content.content:
1	# Data Lineage Trust Platform
2	
3	Backend service for managing datasets, their immutable schema versions and
4	field-level lineage between schema versions. All metadata is persisted in a
5	SQLite database, so data created before a restart remains queryable afterwards.
6	
7	## Requirements
8	
9	- Python 3.12+
10	
11	## Install and test
12	
13	```bash
14	python -m pip install -e '.[dev]'
15	python -m pytest
16	```
17	
18	## Start
19	
20	```bash
21	python -m uvicorn app.main:app --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8000
22	```
23	
24	The SQLite database is stored at `data/lineage.db` by default. Override the
25	location with the `DATA_LINEAGE_DB` environment variable.
26	
27	## Public API
28	
29	All endpoints return JSON. Error responses use the stable shape
30	`{"error": "<code>", "detail": "<message>"}` and never expose SQL or stack
31	traces.
32	
33	### Health
34	
35	- `GET /health` returns `{"status":"ok"}` when the service is ready.
36	
37	### Datasets
38	
39	- `POST /datasets` — create a dataset. Body: `{"name": "orders", "description": "optional"}`.
40	  Returns `201` with `id`, `name`, `description`, `created_at`. Empty name →
41	  `422`; duplicate name → `409`.
42	- `GET /datasets` — list all datasets.
43	
44	### Schema versions (immutable, numbered from 1 per dataset)
45	
46	- `POST /datasets/{dataset}/versions` — create the next schema version. Body:
47	  `{"fields": [{"name": "id", "type": "integer", "nullable": false}]}`.
48	  Field list must be non-empty, field `name`/`type`/`nullable` are required and
49	  field names must be unique within the version. Unknown dataset → `404`;
50	  invalid fields → `422` (nothing is written).
51	- `GET /datasets/{dataset}/versions` — list all versions of a dataset with
52	  their fields.
53	- `GET /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}` — read one version with its
54	  fields. Unknown dataset/version → `404`.
55	- `GET /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{base_version}/compatibility/{target_version}` —
56	  read-only breaking-change check of the target version against the base
57	  version, computed fresh from the persisted field definitions on every read
58	  (nothing is written; field order is not a difference). The endpoint takes no
59	  request body and no query parameters (`422`); unknown dataset/version →
60	  `404`, with the same 404-before-422 precedence as the version diff. The JSON
61	  document is deterministic (fixed key order, compact whitespace, exactly one
62	  trailing newline) with top-level keys `base_version`, `target_version`,
63	  `breaking_changes` and `breaking_change_count`. A breaking change is exactly
64	  one of: the target removed a base field (`removed`), changed a field's type
65	  (`type_changed`) or tightened a nullable field to not nullable
66	  (`nullable_tightened`); added fields and nullable loosening are not
67	  breaking. Each entry has `field`, `kind`, `before` (base definition) and
68	  `after` (target definition, `null` for a removed field), entries are sorted
69	  by field name ascending and `breaking_change_count` equals the number of
70	  entries. Comparing a version with itself returns an empty list and a zero
71	  count. The verdict is advisory for release decisions only: it runs no
72	  migration or rollback.
73	- `GET /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{base_version}/compatibility/{target_version}/impact` —
74	  read-only companion of the compatibility check: the same top-level keys
75	  (`base_version`, `target_version`, `breaking_changes`,
76	  `breaking_change_count`) and the same breaking entries, each entry carrying
77	  one extra key `impacted` after `after`. `impacted` lists every field
78	  directly or indirectly downstream of the broken field along the lineage
79	  mappings, starting from the base version's same-named field and — when the
80	  field still exists in the target version — also from the target version's
81	  field. Each item is `{"dataset", "version", "field"}`; the set is
82	  deduplicated, never contains a start field itself (cycles terminate) and is
83	  sorted by dataset, version and field ascending. A field with no downstream
84	  yields an empty list. The endpoint takes no request body and no query
85	  parameters (`422`); unknown dataset/version → `404` with the same
86	  404-before-422 precedence as the compatibility check, and the JSON document
87	  is deterministic (fixed key order, compact whitespace, exactly one trailing
88	  newline). The read is fully side-effect free: version definitions, lineage
89	  mappings and the impact cache are never written.
90	- `GET /datasets/{dataset}/evolution-summary` — read-only whole-dataset
91	  summary of adjacent-version breaking changes and their downstream impact,
92	  computed fresh on every read (no caching; nothing is written, and version
93	  definitions, lineage mappings and the impact cache are never touched).
94	  Quality and privacy state play no role. The path carries only the dataset
95	  name; the request takes no body and no query parameters (`422`); an unknown
96	  dataset → `404`, with the same 404-before-422 precedence as the
97	  compatibility reads. A dataset with fewer than two versions returns `200`
98	  with an empty `pairs` array and all-zero totals, never an error. The JSON
99	  document is deterministic (fixed key order, compact whitespace, exactly one
100	  trailing newline) with top-level keys `dataset`, `pairs` and `totals`.
101	  `pairs` is ordered by base version number ascending and lists every
102	  adjacent version pair, including pairs without breaking changes; each entry
103	  has exactly `base_version`, `target_version`, `breaking_count`,
104	  `impacted_count` and `impacted_datasets` in that order. `breaking_count` is
105	  the number of breaking entries of the pair, judged exactly as in the
106	  pairwise compatibility impact response (`removed`, `type_changed` or
107	  `nullable_tightened`; several changes of one field collapse into a single
108	  entry). The pair's impacted set is the union of every breaking entry's
109	  downstream fields — same start-field rule as the pairwise impact response,
110	  merged and deduplicated, never containing a start field itself (cycles
111	  terminate) — `impacted_count` is its size and `impacted_datasets` lists the
112	  distinct dataset names appearing in it, sorted ascending. `totals` has
113	  exactly `pair_count` (the number of pairs), `breaking_count` and
114	  `impacted_count`, each the sum of the per-pair values over the whole
115	  dataset.
116	- `GET /datasets/{dataset}/fields/{field}/trajectory` — read-only
117	  cross-version trajectory of one named field of the dataset, computed fresh
118	  on every read (no caching; nothing is written, and version definitions,
119	  lineage mappings and the impact cache are never touched). Only the
120	  persisted version field definitions and lineage mappings are read; quality,
121	  privacy, snapshot and processing-task state play no role. The path carries
122	  the dataset name and the field name; the request takes no body and no query
123	  parameters (`422`); an unknown dataset → `404`, and a field that does not
124	  appear in any of the dataset's versions → `404`, both with the same
125	  404-before-422 precedence as the evolution summary. A dataset with fewer
126	  than two versions returns `200` with an empty `changes` array, never an
127	  error. The JSON document is deterministic (fixed key order, compact
128	  whitespace, exactly one trailing newline) with top-level keys `dataset`,
129	  `field`, `entries` and `changes` in that order. `entries` lists every
130	  schema version of the dataset ordered by version number ascending; each
131	  entry has exactly `version` and `definition`, where `definition` is the
132	  field's persisted definition in that version (`type` and `nullable` only)
133	  or `null` — the key is never omitted — when the field does not exist
134	  there. `changes` lists one entry per adjacent version pair, ordered by
135	  base version ascending; each entry has exactly `base_version`,
136	  `target_version`, `status`, `impacted` and `impacted_datasets` in that
137	  order. `status` reuses the breaking-entry vocabulary of the compatibility
138	  check — `added` (the field appears on the target side), `removed` (it
139	  disappears on the target side), `type_changed`, `nullable_tightened` —
140	  extended with `nullable_loosened` (only the nullability relaxes) and
141	  `unchanged` (both definitions agree, including both absent); a field that
142	  both changes type and tightens nullability collapses into a single
143	  `type_changed` status. `impacted` lists every field directly or indirectly
144	  downstream of the tracked field for that pair along the lineage mappings,
145	  with the same start-field rule as the pairwise compatibility impact
146	  response (the base version's same-named field and, when it exists, the
147	  target version's); each item is `{"dataset", "version", "field"}`, the set
148	  is deduplicated, never contains a start field itself (cycles terminate),
149	  is sorted by dataset, version and field ascending and is empty when the
150	  field has no downstream. `impacted_datasets` lists the distinct dataset
151	  names appearing in `impacted`, sorted ascending.
152	
153	### Field-level lineage
154	
155	A lineage link maps one field of a target schema version to one field of a
156	schema version in a different (source) dataset.
157	
158	- `POST /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/lineage` — register a mapping.
159	  Body names both ends:
160	
161	  ```json
162	  {
163	    "target_dataset": "dm_orders",
164	    "target_version": 1,
165	    "target_field": "id",
166	    "source_dataset": "raw_orders",
167	    "source_version": 1,
168	    "source_field": "order_id"
169	  }
170	  ```
171	
172	  Target must match the path. Source and target datasets must differ and every
173	  referenced dataset/version/field must exist (`404` / `422` otherwise).
174	  Submitting the same complete mapping twice returns `409`.
175	- `DELETE /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/lineage` — remove one
176	  registered mapping. Same address and same body shape as registration: the
177	  six locating fields name the complete mapping to delete and the body target
178	  must match the path. Every locating value readable in the request is
179	  resolved first, so an unknown dataset, version or field is a `404` ahead of
180	  every request-shape error; when all six values name existing resources but
181	  the mapping itself was never registered, the delete is likewise a `404`.
182	  An empty or whitespace body, invalid JSON, a non-object payload, missing or
183	  extra fields, wrongly typed values, blank names, any query parameter, a
184	  mapping whose source and target datasets coincide or whose body target
185	  disagrees with the path are all `422`. No rejection changes the lineage
186	  graph, the impact cache or any other metadata. A registered mapping is
187	  deleted atomically and returns `200` with the removed mapping in the
188	  registration response shape; concurrent deletes of the same mapping succeed
189	  exactly once (the loser gets `404` and changes nothing). The deletion is
190	  visible to every lineage read immediately and survives restarts; the cached
191	  impacts of the mapping's source field and of every field that can reach it
192	  are invalidated exactly as on registration, unrelated entries are kept.
193	- `GET /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/lineage` — return every target
194	  field (including fields without sources) together with its source references.
195	  Results are sorted by target field name, then source dataset name, source
196	  version and source field name.
197	- `GET /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/lineage/impact?field=<field>` —
198	  return the downstream impact of one source field. The path and the `field`
199	  query parameter together name an existing field; the response is
200	  `{"source": {...}, "impacted": [...]}` where `impacted` lists every field
201	  reachable from the source along lineage mappings (direct and indirect), each
202	  entry being `{"dataset", "version", "field"}`. Results are deduplicated,
203	  never contain the source itself (cycles terminate) and are sorted by dataset,
204	  version and field ascending. Unknown dataset/version/field → `404`; a
205	  missing, blank, invalid or repeated `field` parameter → `422` (a repeated
206	  `field` is judged before the field lookup, so it is always a `422`, never a
207	  field `404`).
208	- `GET /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/lineage/impact/cache-audit` —
209	  read-only consistency audit of the version's impact cache, appended one
210	  segment after the impact query address. The path dataset and version name
211	  the audit scope; every field of that version is checked against its current
212	  cache record and recomputed fresh from the committed lineage graph using
213	  exactly the impact-query semantics (downstream fields merged and
214	  deduplicated, the start field excluded, cycles terminating). Each entry is
215	  `{"field", "status"}` with `cached` (the stored record equals the
216	  recomputed result), `missing` (no cache record because the field's impact
217	  was never queried — a normal state, not an error) or `mismatch` (the stored
218	  record differs). Entries are sorted by field name ascending and the sort
219	  does not depend on database order. The JSON document is deterministic
220	  (fixed key order, compact whitespace, exactly one trailing newline) with
221	  top-level keys `dataset`, `version`, `entries` and `counts` in that order;
222	  `counts` gives `cached_count`, `missing_count` and `mismatch_count`, each
223	  equal to the number of entries with that status. The audit is computed on
224	  every read and never writes: no cache record is inserted, invalidated or
225	  repaired, so impact queries, impact paths and source paths behave exactly
226	  as before. The endpoint takes no request body and no query parameters; any
227	  body bytes (whitespace-only included) or query parameter → `422`, and an
228	  unknown dataset or version → `404`, with `404` taking precedence over
229	  `422` as in the impact query.
230	- `POST /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/lineage/impact/cache-audit/repair`
231	  — controlled repair of the version's impact cache, appended one segment
232	  after the read-only audit address and accepting POST only. Every field of
233	  the version is recomputed against the committed lineage graph with the
234	  exact impact-query semantics: a field without a cache record gets one
235	  (`created`), a stored record that disagrees is rewritten (`updated`) and a
236	  matching record is left untouched (`unchanged`). Entries are sorted by
237	  field name ascending and the JSON document is deterministic (fixed key
238	  order, compact whitespace, exactly one trailing newline) with top-level
239	  keys `dataset`, `version`, `entries` and `counts` in that order; each
240	  entry has exactly `field` and `action`, and `counts` gives
241	  `created_count`, `updated_count` and `unchanged_count`. Written records
242	  are ordinary cache rows visible immediately to impact queries and
243	  surviving restarts; a subsequent audit reports every field as `cached`.
244	  The endpoint takes no request body and no query parameters — any body
245	  bytes (whitespace-only included) or query parameter → `422`, an unknown
246	  dataset or version → `404` (with `404` taking precedence as in the audit),
247	  and concurrent repairs of the same version have a single winner, the
248	  loser receiving `409` and changing nothing. Every rejection writes
249	  nothing; lineage registrations and deletions, impact queries, path
250	  explanations, source-path reads and the read-only audit are unaffected.
251	- `GET /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/lineage/impact/cache-invalidations`
252	  — read-only invalidation trail of the version's impact cache, appended one
253	  segment after the impact query address and accepting GET only. Whenever a
254	  lineage mapping is successfully registered or deleted, every invalidated
255	  field that actually had a cache record (the mapping's source field and
256	  every field that can reach it) leaves one append-only record under its own
257	  dataset and version; cache invalidation triggered by schema version
258	  creation leaves no trail. Each entry has exactly `sequence`, `cause`,
259	  `field` and `created_at` in that order: `sequence` numbers the version's
260	  records from 1 in write order (continuous, never reused, even under
261	  concurrent registrations and deletions), `cause` is `registered` or
262	  `deleted` after the triggering mapping write and `created_at` is the
263	  timezone-bearing write time. Entries are sorted by sequence ascending and
264	  a version without records returns an empty `entries` array, never an
265	  error. The JSON document is deterministic (fixed key order, compact
266	  whitespace, exactly one trailing newline) with top-level keys `dataset`,
267	  `version` and `entries` in that order. The trail is append-only and
268	  survives restarts; the read only reads persisted records and never writes,
269	  invalidates or repairs anything. The endpoint takes no request body and no
270	  query parameters; any body bytes (whitespace-only included) or query
271	  parameter → `422`, and an unknown dataset or version → `404`, with `404`
272	  taking precedence over `422` as in the impact query.
273	- `GET /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/lineage/impact-paths?field=<field>` —
274	  read-only shortest-path explanation of the same impact, computed fresh on
275	  every read (no caching; nothing is written, and version definitions, lineage
276	  mappings and the impact cache are never touched). The path and the `field`
277	  query parameter together name an existing field. The JSON document is
278	  deterministic (fixed key order, compact whitespace, exactly one trailing
279	  newline) with top-level keys `source`, `impacts`, `direct_count` and
280	  `indirect_count` in that order; `source` is the start field reference
281	  (`{"dataset", "version", "field"}`). Each `impacts` entry has exactly the
282	  location keys `dataset`, `version`, `field`, then `path` and `path_length`;
283	  entries are deduplicated, never contain the source and are sorted by dataset,
284	  version and field ascending. `path` is the shortest node sequence from the
285	  source to the field, including both ends, and each node has the same
286	  `{"dataset", "version", "field"}` shape; `path_length` is the number of
287	  edges on the path (`1` for a direct downstream field, increasing for
288	  indirect ones). Among several shortest paths, the lexicographically smallest
289	  node sequence (compared by dataset, version and field) is chosen; cycles
290	  terminate. `direct_count` counts fields at distance 1 and `indirect_count`
291	  the fields farther away, and a field with no downstream returns an empty
292	  `impacts` array and both counts zero, never an error. The endpoint takes no
293	  request body and no query parameter other than `field` (a missing, blank or
294	  repeated `field` is likewise a `422`); unknown dataset/version/field →
295	  `404`, with `404` taking precedence over every `422` except that a repeated
296	  `field` is judged before the field lookup and is therefore always a `422`.
297	- `GET /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/lineage/impact/source-paths?field=<field>` —
298	  read-only upstream companion of the lineage impact query, computed fresh on
299	  every read (no caching; nothing is written, and version definitions, lineage
300	  mappings and the impact cache are never touched). The path and the `field`
301	  query parameter together name an existing field; the `field` value is
302	  matched literally (never trimmed), so a whitespace-padded name that matches
303	  no stored field is a `404`. The JSON document is deterministic (fixed key
304	  order, compact whitespace, exactly one trailing newline) with top-level keys
305	  `source`, `origins`, `direct_count`, `indirect_count` and
306	  `source_dataset_count` in that order; `source` is the start field reference
307	  (`{"dataset", "version", "field"}`). Each `origins` entry has exactly the
308	  location keys `dataset`, `version`, `field`, then `path` and `path_length`;
309	  entries are deduplicated, never contain the start field and are sorted by
310	  dataset, version and field ascending. An origin is a field whose mapping
311	  points (directly or transitively) at the start field. `path` is the
312	  shortest node sequence walking from the start field up to the origin,
313	  including both ends, and each node has the same
314	  `{"dataset", "version", "field"}` shape; `path_length` is the number of
315	  edges on the path (`1` for a direct source, increasing for indirect ones).
316	  Among several shortest paths, the lexicographically smallest node sequence
317	  (compared by dataset, version and field) is chosen; cycles terminate.
318	  `direct_count` counts origins at distance 1, `indirect_count` the origins
319	  farther away and `source_dataset_count` the distinct dataset names among
320	  all origins; a field with no sources returns an empty `origins` array and
321	  all counts zero, never an error. The endpoint takes no request body and no
322	  query parameter other than `field` (a missing, blank or repeated `field` is
323	  likewise a `422`); unknown dataset/version/field → `404`, with `404`
324	  taking precedence over every `422` except that a repeated `field` is judged
325	  before the field lookup and is therefore always a `422`.
326	
327	  Impact results are cached persistently (they survive restarts) and every
328	  read reflects the currently committed lineage graph: creating a schema
329	  version invalidates the cache entries related to that dataset, and creating
330	  or deleting a lineage mapping invalidates the cached impacts of the
331	  mapping's source field and of every field that can reach it. Unrelated
332	  cache entries are preserved.
333	
334	### Quality rules
335	
336	Quality rules validate rows against a schema version. Rules are version-scoped
337	and persisted (including their enabled state) across restarts.
338	
339	- `POST /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/quality-rules` — create a rule.
340	  Body: `{"name": "id required", "kind": "not_null", "params": {...}}`. Returns
341	  `201` with `id`, `name`, `kind`, `params`, `enabled`, `created_at`; `enabled`
342	  defaults to `true`. Rule names must be unique within a version (`409` on
343	  conflict). Referenced dataset/version/field must exist (`404`); other invalid
344	  input returns `422` and nothing is written. Supported kinds:
345	  - `not_null` — params `{"field": "<existing field>"}`.
346	  - `numeric_range` — params `{"field": "<existing field>", "min": <finite
347	    number>, "max": <finite number>}` with `min <= max`.
348	  - `unique` — params `{"fields": ["<existing field>", ...]}`: a non-empty list
349	    of distinct, existing field names.
350	- `GET /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/quality-rules` — list rules
351	  sorted by `id` ascending.
352	- `PATCH /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/quality-rules/{rule_id}` —
353	  enable or disable a rule. Body: `{"enabled": true}` (boolean only); returns
354	  the updated rule. Unknown rule/dataset/version → `404`.
355	- `POST /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/quality-rules/evaluate` —
356	  evaluate rows. Body: `{"rows": [{...}, ...]}`. Only enabled rules run.
357	  Returns `{"dataset", "version", "results"}` with results sorted by `rule_id`;
358	  each result has `rule_id`, `name`, `passed` and `violations` (0-based row
359	  indices in ascending order).
360	  - `not_null` fails on missing or `null` values.
361	  - `numeric_range` fails on missing, `null`, non-numeric, boolean or
362	    out-of-range values (boundaries included).
363	  - `unique` compares the tuple of `fields` values per row; a missing field
364	    counts as `null`, and every row taking part in a duplicate group is a
365	    violation.
366	  - With an empty `rows` list every rule passes.
367	- `GET /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/quality-rules/evaluations` —
368	  list the persisted evaluation history of the version, ordered by `sequence`
369	  (occurrence order). Every successful evaluation appends one immutable
370	  summary (`sequence`, `dataset`, `version`, `row_count`,
371	  `violation_row_count` — the number of distinct submitted rows violating at
372	  least one rule — `results` and `created_at`); rejected or failed
373	  evaluations leave no record, and an empty `rows` submission is recorded
374	  with zero violations. The endpoint takes no request body and no query
375	  parameters (`422`); unknown dataset/version → `404`.
376	- `GET /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/quality-rules/evaluations/diff`
377	  — read-only diff between the two most recent recorded evaluations
378	  (`from_sequence` → `to_sequence`). `added_violation_rows` /
379	  `removed_violation_rows` are the 0-based row indices that started or
380	  stopped violating any rule, and each entry of `rules` carries the rule's
381	  `before`/`after` side (`violation_count` and `violations`), the per-rule
382	  `added_violations` / `removed_violations` and the numeric
383	  `violation_count_delta` (negative, zero or positive). A rule missing from
384	  one side (disabled or created between the two evaluations) has a `null`
385	  side and `null` row-level diff fields. With fewer than two recorded
386	  evaluations the response is an explicit empty result (null sequences,
387	  empty lists), not an error. Same `404`/`422` rules as the history
388	  endpoint; nothing is written.
389	
390	### Quality anomaly detection
391	
392	Anomaly detection runs over the persisted evaluation history of a schema
393	version. A version carries at most one detection config; scans append
394	immutable anomaly records that persist across restarts.
395	
396	- `POST /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/quality-rules/anomaly-detection`
397	  — register the version's detection config. The body contains exactly three
398	  integers: `consecutive_worsening_steps` (at least `2`),
399	  `violation_row_limit` and `rule_violation_limit` (both non-negative).
400	  Returns `201` with the config (`id`, `dataset`, `version`, the three
401	  thresholds, `created_at`). A second config for the same version returns
402	  `409`; unknown dataset/version → `404`; missing, extra, non-integer or
403	  out-of-range fields → `422` and nothing is written.
404	- `GET /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/quality-rules/anomaly-detection`
405	  — return the registered config (`404` when none exists). The endpoint takes
406	  no request body and no query parameters (`422`).
407	- `POST /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/quality-rules/anomaly-detection/scan`
408	  — run one detection pass over the persisted evaluation history and return
409	  the anomaly records this scan newly added (ordered by `id`); they are
410	  persisted in the same transaction. Scanning without a registered config
411	  returns `409`; an empty history is a successful scan that writes nothing.
412	  The endpoint takes no request body and no query parameters (`422`). Each
413	  record has `id`, `kind`, `sequence` (the history sequence it points to),
414	  `rule_id`, `violation_count` and `created_at`; `kind` is one of:
415	  - `row_limit` — the evaluation's `violation_row_count` exceeds
416	    `violation_row_limit` (`rule_id` is `null`).
417	  - `rule_limit` — one rule's violation count in the evaluation exceeds
418	    `rule_violation_limit`; `rule_id` carries the rule's id.
419	  - `trend` — the violation row counts of adjacent evaluations strictly
420	    increase and the consecutive increase count at the tail of the history
421	    reaches `consecutive_worsening_steps`; the record points to the final
422	    evaluation of the increasing sequence (`rule_id` is `null`). A shorter
423	    run or any decline produces no trend record.
424	
425	  A record with the same kind, history sequence and rule id is never
426	  duplicated: repeated scans only persist and return newly appearing
427	  anomalies, and concurrent scans store each anomaly exactly once with
428	  contiguous ids.
429	- `GET /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/quality-rules/anomaly-detection/anomalies`
430	  — list every anomaly record of the version sorted by `id` ascending (empty
431	  when there are none, never an error). Same `404`/`422` rules as the scan
432	  endpoint; nothing is written.
433	
434	### Quality gate
435	
436	The quality gate is the release-readiness verdict of a schema version. It is
437	computed fresh from the persisted records on every read — nothing is cached,
438	re-run or written, and the rule definitions are never consulted (violations
439	recorded for rules since disabled still count).
440	
441	- `GET /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/quality-rules/gate` — return the
442	  verdict as a deterministic JSON document (fixed key order, compact
443	  whitespace, exactly one trailing newline):
444	  `{"dataset", "version", "verdict", "reasons", "counts"}`.
445	  - `verdict` is one of:
446	    - `pass` — the latest recorded evaluation passed every rule and no
447	      anomaly record exists; a zero-violation evaluation left by an empty
448	      `rows` submission is a valid basis.
449	    - `undetermined` — no evaluation was ever recorded; `reasons` is empty
450	      and the read succeeds (never an error).
451	    - `fail` — the latest recorded evaluation still has violating rows, or
452	      the version carries any anomaly record.
453	  - `reasons` lists every factor that lowers the verdict, sorted by `kind`,
454	    `sequence` and `rule_id` (null ids first), all ascending. Each reason has
455	    `kind`, `sequence`, `rule_id` and `violation_count` (a missing rule id is
456	    `null`, never omitted). Every rule with violations in the latest
457	    evaluation contributes one `violation` reason with its violation row
458	    count; every persisted anomaly record contributes one reason of its own
459	    kind (`row_limit`, `rule_limit` or `trend`). A rule that appears in both
460	    yields two reasons — they are never merged or deduplicated.
461	  - `counts` reports how many persisted records the verdict examined:
462	    `evaluations`, `anomalies` and `reasons` (the length of the reason list).
463	  - The endpoint takes no request body and no query parameters: any body
464	    bytes — including whitespace-only ones — or any query parameter are a
465	    `422`, checked after the path dataset/version resolves (`404` first).
466	    Nothing is written on any rejection.
467	- `GET /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/quality-rules/gate/at?timestamp=...`
468	  — the same verdict as it stood at a requested instant. `timestamp` must be
469	  a timezone-bearing ISO-8601 date-time; only evaluations and anomaly records
470	  written at or before it count, and the latest evaluation of that window is
471	  the one with the highest sequence inside it. The response is the same
472	  deterministic document as the bare gate (`dataset`, `version`, `verdict`,
473	  `reasons`, `counts`, one trailing newline), with the counts covering only
474	  the records inside the window. A window without any evaluation is
475	  `undetermined` with an empty reason list — a normal response, never an
476	  error. The endpoint accepts GET only and is strictly read-only. The path
477	  dataset/version resolves first (`404`); afterwards any request body bytes
478	  (whitespace-only included), a missing, repeated, unparseable or
479	  timezone-less `timestamp`, or any other query parameter are a `422` that
480	  writes nothing.
481	- `GET /datasets/{dataset}/quality-gate-export` — read-only cross-version
482	  export of the dataset's whole quality gate state, computed fresh on every
483	  read (no caching; nothing is written, modified or deleted, and no
484	  evaluation, anomaly record or gate verdict is touched). The path carries
485	  only the dataset name; the request takes no body and no query parameters —
486	  any body bytes, including a purely whitespace or single-space body, or any
487	  query parameter → `422`; an unknown dataset → `404`, checked before the
488	  request shape, with the same 404-before-422 precedence as the compliance
489	  exports. A dataset without schema versions returns `200` with an empty
490	  `versions` array and all-zero totals, never an error. The JSON document is
491	  deterministic (fixed key order, compact whitespace, exactly one trailing
492	  newline):
493	
494	  ```json
495	  {"dataset":"orders","versions":[{"version":1,"verdict":"fail","reason_count":1,"violation_row_count":2},{"version":2,"verdict":"undetermined","reason_count":0,"violation_row_count":null}],"totals":{"version_count":2,"failed_count":1,"reason_count":1,"violation_row_count":2}}
496	  ```
497	
498	  The top-level keys are exactly `dataset`, `versions`, `totals` in that
499	  order. `versions` is ordered by version number ascending and each entry has
500	  exactly `version`, `verdict`, `reason_count` and `violation_row_count` in
501	  that order. `verdict` is the current per-version gate verdict (one of
502	  `pass`, `undetermined`, `fail`) under exactly the same computation as the
503	  per-version gate read; `reason_count` is the number of reasons currently
504	  lowering that verdict (the length of the per-version gate's reason list);
505	  `violation_row_count` is the violation row count of the latest recorded
506	  evaluation and is `null` — never omitted — when the version was never
507	  evaluated. `totals` has exactly `version_count`, `failed_count`,
508	  `reason_count` and `violation_row_count`: the number of version entries,
509	  the number of versions whose verdict is `fail`, and the sums of the
510	  per-version reason and violation row counts (null violation row counts
511	  count as zero).
512	
513	### Privacy policies
514	
515	Privacy policies attach a sensitivity classification and masking strategy to a
516	single field of a schema version, enabling role-based de-identification of row
517	data. Policies (including their enabled state) are persisted across restarts.
518	
519	- `POST /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/privacy-policies` — register a
520	  policy. Body:
521	  `{"field": "email", "classification": "PII", "masking": "partial", "allowed_roles": ["analyst"]}`.
522	  `field` must name an existing field of the version; `classification` is a
523	  non-empty string; `masking` is `redact` or `partial`; `allowed_roles` is an
524	  array of distinct, non-empty role names and may be empty. Returns `201` with
525	  the submitted fields plus `id`, `enabled` (defaults to `true`) and
526	  `created_at`. Registering two policies for the same field within one version
527	  returns `409`. Unknown dataset/version/field → `404`; other invalid input →
528	  `422` and nothing is written.
529	- `GET /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/privacy-policies` — list policies
530	  sorted by `id` ascending.
531	- `PATCH /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/privacy-policies/{policy_id}` —
532	  enable or disable a policy. Body: `{"enabled": true}` (boolean only); returns
533	  the updated policy. Unknown policy/dataset/version → `404`.
534	- `PUT /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/privacy-policies/{policy_id}` —
535	  revise a policy. Body carries exactly the three adjustable fields:
536	  `{"classification": "PII", "masking": "partial", "allowed_roles":
537	  ["analyst"]}`, using the same value rules as registration — a non-empty
538	  `classification` after trimming, `masking` of `redact` or `partial`, and an
539	  `allowed_roles` array of distinct, non-empty-after-trimming role names that
540	  may be empty. The three fields are replaced together from one whole
541	  submission. The revision never changes the policy id, the field it belongs
542	  to, its `enabled` state or its `created_at`; it writes only the policy
543	  itself — no policy is created, no identification record is touched and no
544	  masking suggestion is registered. Returns `200` with the updated policy in
545	  the same shape as the policy read, and the revision survives restarts. The
546	  next privacy view read (and every later masked read) judges each value by
547	  the revised classification, masking and allowed roles. Already-written
548	  masking-hit records, access records and cleanup requests are unaffected —
549	  their contents and ordering stay as written; the grouping of the summary,
550	  diff and reconciliation responses keeps the same counting rules, while the
551	  policy classification and masking reported on trend rows (and the policy
552	  entries of the coverage check and compliance export) reflect the current
553	  values. Advisory masking suggestions are unaffected. Unknown
554	  dataset/version/policy → `404`, judged before every request-shape check;
555	  missing or extra fields, a blank `classification`, an illegal `masking`
556	  value, duplicate or blank `allowed_roles` entries, an empty or
557	  whitespace-only body, malformed JSON, a non-object payload or any query
558	  parameter → `422` and nothing is written. Concurrent revisions of the same
559	  policy have exactly one winner; the loser receives `409` and changes no
560	  field.
561	
562	- `POST /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/privacy-policies/view` — return a
563	  role-scoped, order-preserving copy of submitted rows. Body:
564	  `{"role": "guest", "rows": [{...}, ...]}` with a non-empty `role` and a list
565	  of row objects. Response: `{"dataset", "version", "rows"}`. Only enabled
566	  policies whose field appears in a row mask the value when `role` is not in
567	  `allowed_roles`:
568	  - `redact` replaces every non-`null` value with `"***"`.
569	  - `partial` keeps the first character and last two characters of strings
570	    longer than 4 characters (e.g. `"alice@example.com"` → `"aom"`); every other
571	    non-`null` value (short strings, numbers, booleans, …) is replaced with
572	    `"***"`.
573	  - `null` values and fields without a policy are returned unchanged; rows
574	    missing a covered field are left without it.
575	
576	  Every successful view also appends one audit record per value it actually
577	  masked (the same field masked in several rows yields one record per masked
578	  value; a role in `allowed_roles`, a `null` value, an uncovered field or a
579	  disabled policy never hits); the records are persisted per version and are
580	  append-only.
581	
582	  Every successful view additionally appends exactly one access record,
583	  whether or not it masked any value (an empty `rows` submission is recorded
584	  too). Rejected or failed views leave neither kind of record.
585	- `GET /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/privacy-policies/view/access-records`
586	  — list every access record of the version, ordered by `sequence` ascending
587	  (empty when there are none, never an error). Each record has `sequence`,
588	  `role`, `row_count` (the number of submitted rows), `masked_count` (the
589	  number of masking-hit records the same view wrote, so the two logs
590	  cross-check) and `created_at`. The endpoint takes no request body and no
591	  query parameters (`422`); unknown dataset/version → `404`. Nothing is
592	  written.
593	- `GET /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/privacy-policies/view/audit-records`
594	  — list every masking-hit record of the version, ordered by `sequence`
595	  ascending (empty when there are none, never an error). Each record has
596	  `sequence`, `field`, `policy_id`, `role`, `masking` and `created_at`. The
597	  endpoint takes no request body and no query parameters (`422`); unknown
598	  dataset/version → `404`. Nothing is written.
599	- `GET /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/privacy-policies/view/audit-records/search`
600	  — read-only filtered retrieval of the same masking-hit records. The
601	  response is the same record collection as the full list (each record has
602	  `sequence`, `field`, `policy_id`, `role`, `masking` and `created_at`),
603	  sorted by `sequence` ascending; a filter that matches nothing returns an
604	  empty array, never an error. All filters are optional query parameters and
605	  combine with AND:
606	  - `role` — exact match against the requesting role recorded on the hit,
607	    case-insensitive (no substring or other fuzzy matching).
608	  - `field` — exact match against the hit field name, case-insensitive.
609	  - `start` / `end` — closed write-time interval: a record matches when its
610	    `created_at` is between the bounds inclusive. Each bound is a
611	    timezone-bearing ISO-8601 date-time (offset or `Z`); either bound may be
612	    given alone. `start` later than `end` → `422`.
613	
614	  The endpoint takes no request body; an unparseable or timezone-less
615	  `start`/`end`, or any query parameter other than `role`, `field`, `start`
616	  and `end`, → `422`. Unknown dataset/version → `404`, with the same
617	  404-before-422 precedence as the record list. It is strictly read-only:
618	  no record is written, modified or deleted and the summary/diff responses
619	  are unaffected.
620	- `GET /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/privacy-policies/view/audit-records/summary`
621	  — read-only compliance summary computed fresh from the persisted records on
622	  every read (no caching, nothing is written or deleted). Response:
623	  `{"dataset", "version", "groups"}`; `groups` is an empty array when the
624	  version has no records. Each group merges records with the same `field`,
625	  `policy_id`, `role` and `masking` (different roles or masking modes stay
626	  separate) and lists `field`, `policy_id`, `role`, `masking`, `hit_count`
627	  (one record counts as one hit), `first_hit_at` and `last_hit_at` (the
628	  earliest and latest record `created_at` in the group). Groups sort by
629	  `field`, then `policy_id`, `role` and `masking`, all ascending. The
630	  endpoint takes no request body and no query parameters (`422`); unknown
631	  dataset/version → `404`, with the same 404-before-422 precedence as the
632	  record list.
633	- `GET /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/privacy-policies/view/audit-records/trend`
634	  — read-only hit trend aggregated by privacy policy, computed fresh from the
635	  persisted records on every read (no caching, nothing is written or deleted).
636	  Hits of the same policy merge across roles (a disabled policy's historical
637	  hits still count). Response: `{"dataset", "version", "policies", "totals"}`;
638	  `policies` is an empty array when the version has no records. Each policy
639	  row carries `policy_id`, `field`, `classification`, `masking`, `total_hits`
640	  and `days`; policies sort by `policy_id` ascending. `days` lists only UTC
641	  calendar days with hits (a write time with a non-zero offset buckets by its
642	  UTC day), sorted ascending with no zero-filled gaps; each entry has `day`
643	  (`YYYY-MM-DD`), `hit_count` (one record counts once), `hit_count_delta`
644	  (difference from the previous listed day, `null` on the first) and `trend`
645	  (`up`/`down`/`flat`, or `none` on the first day). `totals` gives
646	  `total_hits` (the sum of the row totals), `policy_count` (policies with
647	  hits) and `day_count` (distinct hit days over the whole version, the
648	  per-policy day union). The endpoint takes no request body and no query
649	  parameters (`422`); unknown dataset/version → `404`, with the same
650	  404-before-422 precedence as the record list.
651	- `POST /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/privacy-policies/view/audit-records/cleanup-requests`
652	  — open a two-stage retention cleanup request for the version's masking-hit
653	  records. Body contains exactly `reason` and `before`:
654	  `{"reason": "legal hold expired", "before": "2026-01-01T00:00:00Z"}`.
655	  `reason` must be a string that is non-empty after trimming whitespace;
656	  `before` must be an ISO-8601 date-time carrying a timezone (offset or `Z`),
657	  and a record belongs to the target set only when its hit write time is
658	  strictly earlier than that instant. Creating a request only returns a
659	  preview — no hit record is deleted or modified, and the record list,
660	  search, summary, diff, reconcile and trend responses stay unchanged.
661	  Returns `201` with `id`, `reason` (trimmed), `before` (echoed as
662	  submitted), `status` (`pending`), `created_at` and a `preview` block:
663	  `hit_count` (the number of records that would be cleaned up),
664	  `first_hit_at` / `last_hit_at` (the earliest and latest hit times in the
665	  target set, `null` when the set is empty) and `fields` (the distinct field
666	  names involved, sorted ascending; `[]` when empty). The target set is
667	  fixed at creation time: masking-hit records written afterwards never enter
668	  the request even when they precede the cutoff by clock time. At most one
669	  pending request may exist per version; creating another while one is open
670	  returns `409` and writes nothing (confirmed requests never block a new
671	  one). Unknown dataset/version → `404`; missing/non-string/blank `reason`,
672	  missing/unparseable/timezone-less `before`, an extra body field, a
673	  non-JSON/non-object body or any query parameter → `422` and nothing is
674	  written, with 404 taking precedence.
675	- `GET .../privacy-policies/view/audit-records/cleanup-requests` — list the
676	  version's cleanup requests sorted by request `id` ascending (empty when
677	  there are none). Confirmed requests stay listed and requests survive
678	  process restarts. The endpoint takes no request body and no query
679	  parameters (`422`); unknown dataset/version → `404`.
680	- `POST .../privacy-policies/view/audit-records/cleanup-requests/{request_id}/confirm`
681	  — confirm a request with an empty request body and no query parameters.
682	  Confirmation atomically deletes exactly the target set frozen at creation
683	  and sets `status` to `confirmed`; the response is the request plus
684	  `confirmed_at` and `deleted_count` (the number of records actually
685	  deleted, possibly zero). Confirming an already-confirmed request returns
686	  `409` and never changes data again; concurrent confirmations have exactly
687	  one winner (the others get `409`) and can never leave the records half
688	  deleted. After a cleanup the surviving hit records keep their original
689	  `sequence` numbers and later hits continue the existing increasing run
690	  without reusing cleaned numbers; the record list and search return only
691	  surviving records, and summary, trend, diff and reconcile recompute from
692	  them. Access records are not cleaned up and the processing-task audit
693	  chain remains immutable. A request body or query parameter on the confirm
694	  endpoint → `422`; unknown dataset/version/request → `404` (precedence
695	  matches the hit-record reads), and confirming a confirmed request →
696	  `409`.
697	- `GET /datasets/{dataset}/privacy-compliance-export` — read-only
698	  cross-version export of the dataset's whole privacy compliance state,
699	  computed fresh on every read (no caching; nothing is written, modified or
700	  deleted, and no hit record, access record or cleanup request is touched).
701	  The path carries only the dataset name; the request takes no body and no
702	  query parameters (`422`); an unknown dataset → `404`, with the same
703	  404-before-422 precedence as the hit-record reads. A dataset without
704	  schema versions returns `200` with an empty `versions` array and all-zero
705	  totals, never an error. The JSON document is deterministic (fixed key
706	  order, compact whitespace, exactly one trailing newline):
707	
708	  ```json
709	  {"dataset":"orders","versions":[{"version":1,"policies":[...],"hit_count":0,"masked_count":1,"view_count":2,"cleanup_requests":[...]}],"totals":{...}}
710	  ```
711	
712	  The top-level keys are exactly `dataset`, `versions`, `totals` in that
713	  order. `versions` is ordered by version number ascending and each entry
714	  has exactly `version`, `policies`, `hit_count`, `masked_count`,
715	  `view_count`, `cleanup_requests` in that order. `policies` lists the
716	  version's registered policies ordered by policy id; each policy has `id`,
717	  `field`, `classification`, `masking`, `allowed_roles` and `enabled`.
718	  `cleanup_requests` lists the version's cleanup requests ordered by request
719	  id (both pending and confirmed are retained); each has `id`, `reason`,
720	  `status` and `created_at`. `hit_count` is the number of masking-hit
721	  records currently stored for the version, `masked_count` is the sum of the
722	  access records' masked-value counts and `view_count` is the number of
723	  access records; all three reflect the records surviving a confirmed
724	  cleanup. `totals` has exactly `policy_count`, `hit_count`, `masked_count`,
725	  `view_count` and `cleanup_request_count`, each the sum of the per-version
726	  values over the whole dataset.
727	- `GET /datasets/{dataset}/privacy-policy-coverage` — read-only cross-version
728	  check of the dataset's privacy policy coverage, computed fresh on every
729	  read (no caching; nothing is written, modified or deleted, and no policy
730	  or identification record is touched). The path carries only the dataset
731	  name; the request takes no body and no query parameters (`422`); an
732	  unknown dataset → `404`, with the same 404-before-422 precedence as the
733	  compliance export. A dataset without schema versions returns `200` with an
734	  empty `versions` array and all-zero totals, never an error. The JSON
735	  document is deterministic (fixed key order, compact whitespace, exactly
736	  one trailing newline):
737	
738	  ```json
739	  {"dataset":"orders","versions":[{"version":1,"fields":[...],"candidates":[...]}],"totals":{...}}
740	  ```
741	
742	  The top-level keys are exactly `dataset`, `versions`, `totals` in that
743	  order. `versions` is ordered by version number ascending and each entry
744	  has exactly `version`, `fields`, `candidates` in that order. `fields`
745	  lists every field of the version ordered by field name; each entry has
746	  `field`, `coverage`, `classification`, `masking` and `enabled`, where
747	  `coverage` is `enabled` (an enabled policy is registered), `disabled` (a
748	  policy is registered but disabled) or `unregistered` (no policy), and the
749	  last three keys report the registered policy's classification, masking and
750	  enabled state (all `null` when no policy is registered). `candidates`
751	  lists the advisory suggestions for fields that were identified with at
752	  least one name or sample hit but carry no privacy policy yet, ordered by
753	  identification record id ascending; each candidate has exactly `field`,
754	  `classification` and `masking`, and an identified field whose name and
755	  samples both missed does not appear. The candidates are a compliance
756	  self-check reference only: they never register a policy and never rewrite
757	  an identification record. `totals` has exactly `version_count`,
758	  `field_count`, `enabled_count`, `disabled_count`, `unregistered_count`
759	  and `candidate_count`, each the sum of the per-version values over the
760	  whole dataset.
761	
762	### Sensitive-field identification
763	
764	Sensitive-field identification produces candidate annotations for the fields of
765	a schema version. It complements the manual privacy policies but never creates
766	or modifies one: an identification is advisory only. Records (including their
767	stable ids) persist across restarts.
768	
769	- `POST /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/sensitive-identifications` —
770	  identify one field. The body contains exactly `field` and `samples`:
771	  `{"field": "contact_email", "samples": ["alice@example.com"]}`. `field` must
772	  name an existing field of the version; its name and type are taken from the
773	  version definition. `samples` is an array of JSON scalars (strings, numbers,
774	  booleans or `null`) and may be empty; objects or arrays reject the whole
775	  request. The samples are never stored or echoed back. Returns the record;
776	  the first submission for a field returns `201`, re-running the same field
777	  refreshes the record in place (the id is unchanged) and returns `200`.
778	- `GET /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/sensitive-identifications` —
779	  return every identification record of the version sorted by id ascending
780	  (empty when there are none). The endpoint takes no request body and no query
781	  parameters (`422`); unknown dataset/version → `404`.
782	
783	  Each record has `id`, `field`, `field_type`, `evidence`, `confidence`,
784	  `source` and `created_at`. `source` references the identified field as
785	  `{"dataset", "version", "field"}`. `evidence` is the ordered, de-duplicated
786	  list of hit kinds, name hits before sample hits:
787	
788	  - **Name hits** — the field name contains a sensitive word case-insensitively
789	    as a substring. The words are `email`, `phone`, `id_card`, `password`,
790	    `token` and `birth`, emitting `name:<word>` in that order.
791	  - **Sample hits** — only string sample values are inspected (numbers,
792	    booleans and `null` never hit), and only when the field's declared type is
793	    `string`; a field declared with any other type is matched by name alone,
794	    even when a sample looks like an email. `sample:email` requires exactly
795	    one `@` with non-empty text on both sides and a dot in the domain;
796	    `sample:phone` requires an 11-digit string starting with `1`. Either format
797	    matching is sufficient.
798	
799	  `confidence` is `high` when both the name and the samples hit, `medium` for
800	  samples only, `low` for the name only and `none` when neither side hits
801	  (`evidence` is then an empty list but the record is still generated).
802	
803	  One record is kept per field: a re-run overwrites the evidence and confidence
804	  in place with a stable id. Unknown dataset/version → `404`; a field that does
805	  not exist in the version → `404`; missing or extra body fields, a
806	  non-string or blank field name, a `samples` value that is not an array of
807	  scalars (objects and arrays included), an empty body, malformed JSON or any
808	  query parameter → `422` and nothing is written.
809	
810	#### Masking strategy suggestions
811	
812	- `GET /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/sensitive-identifications/masking-suggestions`
813	  — read-only advisory masking-strategy candidates derived from the version's
814	  identification records. The endpoint takes no request body and no query
815	  parameters (`422` if either is present, with nothing written); unknown
816	  dataset/version → `404`. A version without identification records returns an
817	  empty list rather than an error.
818	
819	  Each candidate has exactly `field`, `classification`, `masking` and
820	  `allowed_roles`. Only records whose name or samples hit produce a candidate;
821	  a record with empty evidence is omitted. Candidates follow the identification
822	  records' `id` ascending and are recomputed on every read, so refreshing an
823	  identification changes the suggestion on the next request. The endpoint
824	  writes nothing, never registers a privacy policy and leaves the
825	  identification records' fields, ordering and refresh semantics untouched;
826	  the privacy view continues to mask according to registered policies only.
827	
828	  - `classification` is `PII` for email, phone, id-card and birthday hits, and
829	    `CREDENTIAL` for password and token hits. A field hitting both is `PII`.
830	  - `masking` reuses the privacy-view vocabulary: `partial` for `PII`
831	    candidates and `redact` for `CREDENTIAL` candidates (a both-kinds field
832	    takes `partial`); no new masking format is introduced.
833	  - `allowed_roles` is always an empty list: the suggested masking applies to
834	    every role, granting none an unmasked view.
835	
836	- `POST /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/sensitive-identifications/masking-suggestions/register`
837	  — turn the current advisory candidates into registered privacy policies. The
838	  body contains only `{"fields": ["<field>", ...]}`: a non-empty array of
839	  distinct field names, each non-empty after trimming and naming an existing
840	  field of the version that currently has a masking suggestion candidate.
841	  Returns `201` with one privacy policy record per requested field, in the
842	  request's field-name order; each record has the same fields as the manual
843	  policy creation response (`id`, `field`, `classification`, `masking`,
844	  `allowed_roles`, `enabled`, `created_at`), is enabled by default and gets a
845	  service-generated id and timestamp. Each policy copies its candidate's
846	  `classification` and `masking` verbatim with the candidate's empty
847	  `allowed_roles`, so after registration every role sees those fields masked;
848	  the next privacy view read masks according to the new policies. The whole
849	  batch is validated before anything is written, so any rejection writes no
850	  policy and no timestamp. Unknown dataset/version, or a named field that does
851	  not exist in the version → `404`; a field without an available candidate
852	  (never identified, or whose identification record currently yields no
853	  candidate) or one that already has a privacy policy → `409`; two concurrent
854	  registrations of the same field leave exactly one winner. Missing or extra
855	  body fields, an empty `fields` array, duplicate, non-string or blank names,
856	  an empty body, a whitespace-only body, malformed JSON or any query parameter
857	  → `422` and nothing is written. Registration only reads the identification
858	  records and field definitions; it never writes or auto-refreshes an
859	  identification, and the read-only suggestions endpoint stays unchanged.
860	
861	### Row snapshots
862	
863	A row snapshot persistently records the rows of a schema version at one point in
864	time. Snapshots (including their rows) survive restarts.
865	
866	- `POST /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/snapshots` — persist a snapshot.
867	  Body: `{"rows": [{...}, ...]}` where `rows` must be an array of JSON objects
868	  (it may be empty). The JSON values and the order of rows/object keys are deep
869	  copied verbatim. A SHA-256 content fingerprint of the saved row sequence is
870	  computed at creation and written together with the rows in one atomic write,
871	  so it can later attest that the persisted rows are unchanged; the fingerprint
872	  is not part of the response, which stays `id`, `dataset`, `version`,
873	  `created_at` and `row_count` (no rows). In the same transaction the service
874	  also maintains the snapshot diff cache incrementally (see "Snapshot diff
875	  cache" below): the canonical form of every row (key-sorted compact JSON text
876	  in stored row order) and the sorted set of top-level field names are written
877	  together with the snapshot, and one `created` record is appended to the
878	  version's cache trail. Unknown dataset/version → `404`; malformed or
879	  non-object rows → `422` and nothing is written.
880	- `GET /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/snapshots` — list snapshot
881	  metadata sorted by `id` ascending (no `rows`).
882	- `GET /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/snapshots/{snapshot_id}` — return
883	  the metadata together with the saved `rows`. Unknown dataset/version/snapshot
884	  → `404`.
885	- `GET /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/snapshots/{snapshot_id}/verify` —
886	  read-only content-fingerprint verification, appended one segment after the
887	  single-snapshot read address and accepting GET only. On every read the
888	  fingerprint of the currently persisted row sequence is recomputed and
889	  compared with the fingerprint stored with the snapshot at creation; the
890	  snapshot and its rows are only read, never written or modified. The JSON
891	  document is deterministic (fixed key order, compact whitespace, lowercase
892	  booleans, exactly one trailing newline) with top-level keys `dataset`,
893	  `version`, `snapshot_id`, `row_count`, `stored_hash`, `computed_hash` and
894	  `valid` in that order. `stored_hash` is the fingerprint written at creation,
895	  `computed_hash` the freshly recomputed one and `valid` is `true` exactly
896	  while both agree; directly changing, adding, deleting or replacing a saved
897	  row makes them differ and changes `computed_hash`. Both verdicts return
898	  `200`. The fingerprint hashes the saved row sequence as a JSON array in row
899	  order with each object's keys sorted by Unicode code point, compact text,
900	  non-ASCII characters unescaped, UTF-8 encoded and SHA-256 digested to
901	  hexadecimal; array order and value types are significant (integers, floats,
902	  strings and booleans never compare equal and negative zero is represented
903	  distinctly), an empty snapshot is fingerprinted normally and the same rows
904	  yield the same digest across restarts. The verification reads only the
905	  snapshot and its rows — no lineage, quality, privacy or task state — and
906	  does not affect retention or deletion; a confirmed-deleted snapshot is no
907	  longer addressable here either (`404`). The endpoint takes no request body
908	  and no query parameters: any body bytes — including whitespace-only ones —
909	  or any query parameter are a `422`, checked after the path
910	  dataset/version/snapshot resolves, so an unknown dataset, version or
911	  snapshot is a `404` first. Every rejection writes nothing.
912	- `GET /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/snapshots/at?timestamp=<ISO-8601>` —
913	  return the most recent snapshot whose `created_at` is not later than
914	  `timestamp`, including its rows. The timestamp must be a timezone-aware
915	  ISO-8601 date-time (an offset or trailing `Z`): missing, invalid or
916	  timezone-less values return `422`; unknown dataset/version → `404`; when no
917	  snapshot exists at or before the timestamp the response is `404`.
918	- `GET /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/snapshots/at/diff?from=<ISO-8601>&to=<ISO-8601>`
919	  — read-only time-travel row diff, appended one segment after the bare-row
920	  time lookup and accepting GET only. Each of `from` (the baseline) and `to`
921	  (the target) must be a timezone-aware ISO-8601 date-time; each side
922	  independently selects the latest snapshot whose `created_at` is not later
923	  than its own timestamp (the same selection as the bare-row lookup), so the
924	  two times may resolve to the same snapshot and a `to` earlier than `from` is
925	  valid — the two snapshots are simply compared in their named order. The
926	  comparison reads snapshots and rows and writes nothing. The JSON document
927	  is deterministic (fixed key order, compact whitespace, exactly one trailing
928	  newline) with top-level keys `from_timestamp`, `to_timestamp`,
929	  `from_snapshot_id`, `to_snapshot_id`, `added`, `removed`, `fields_added`
930	  and `fields_removed` in that order; the timestamps echo the submitted query
931	  values. `added` and `removed` use the exact comparison semantics of the
932	  snapshot-id diff (JSON-object multisets, key order irrelevant, array order
933	  and value types significant, duplicates counted; entries
934	  `{"row", "count"}` sorted by canonical row text). `fields_added` and
935	  `fields_removed` compare the top-level field names appearing on the
936	  snapshots' row objects: names only on the target side are added, names only
937	  on the baseline side are removed, names on both enter neither set, and each
938	  list sorts by field name ascending. When both times select the same
939	  snapshot all four collections are empty and the request succeeds. Unknown
940	  dataset/version → `404`, checked before every request-shape check; a missing,
941	  blank, repeated, unparseable or timezone-less `from`/`to`, an extra query
942	  parameter or any request body bytes (whitespace-only included) → `422`; a
943	  side with no snapshot at or before its timestamp → `404` and nothing is
944	  written.
945	- `POST /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/snapshots/at/diff/masked` —
946	  role-masked time-travel row diff, appended one segment after the bare-row
947	  time diff and accepting POST only. The body contains exactly `role`,
948	  `from` and `to`: `{"role": "guest", "from": "<ISO-8601>", "to":
949	  "<ISO-8601>"}`; `role` must be non-empty after trimming and each time must
950	  be a timezone-aware ISO-8601 date-time (offset or `Z`). Each side
951	  independently selects the newest snapshot whose `created_at` is not later
952	  than its own timestamp, with exactly the same selection as the bare-row
953	  time lookup. Added and removed entries are first judged and counted from
954	  the raw, unmasked rows with the bare-row diff's JSON-object multiset
955	  semantics (key order irrelevant, array order and value types significant,
956	  duplicates counted): a row appearing several times stays one entry with
957	  its multiplicity, and masking only rewrites the entry's row data — entries
958	  are never merged or split. Entries sort by the canonical (key-sorted) JSON
959	  text of the raw row, so the output order is unaffected by masking. Each
960	  emitted row is then masked exactly as the row-submission privacy view masks
961	  it, applying only the version's currently enabled policies
962	  (`redact`/`partial` semantics, `allowed_roles`, nulls and uncovered fields
963	  behave identically). The response is the same deterministic document as
964	  the bare-row time diff (fixed key order, compact whitespace, exactly one
965	  trailing newline) with the same keys in the same order: `from_timestamp`,
966	  `to_timestamp`, `from_snapshot_id`, `to_snapshot_id`, `added`, `removed`,
967	  `fields_added` and `fields_removed`; the timestamps echo the submitted
968	  body values and the field-name sets carry no values, so masking can never
969	  change them. Every successful read appends one masking-hit record per
970	  value it actually masks, counted per occurrence across both snapshots'
971	  diff entries (an entry of count `n` whose covered value is masked yields
972	  `n` hit records; added-side entries first, then removed-side, each side in
973	  canonical row order), structurally identical to the regular view's hit
974	  records and continuing the same per-version sequence run, plus exactly one
975	  access record whose `row_count` is the total number of rows expanded from
976	  both sides' entries and whose `masked_count` equals the number of hit
977	  records the read wrote. The records enter all existing masking-hit/access
978	  reads, filters, summaries, diffs, reconciliation, trends and cleanup
979	  previews; records of one read share a write timestamp, sequences stay
980	  continuous across processes, and a write obstruction never fails the read.
981	  The read never modifies snapshots, rows, policies or identification
982	  records. Unknown dataset/version → `404`; each side with a usable
983	  timestamp is resolved independently, so a side with no snapshot at or
984	  before its timestamp is likewise `404` and precedes every shape check
985	  (including a missing or invalid timestamp on the other side); a missing or
986	  wrong-typed `role`/`from`/`to`, a role blank after trimming, an
987	  unparseable or timezone-less time, an extra body field, an empty,
988	  whitespace-only or non-JSON body, a non-object body and any query
989	  parameter are `422` and write nothing.
990	- `POST /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/snapshots/at/masked-view` —
991	  role-masked time travel, appended one segment after the bare-row time
992	  lookup and accepting POST only. The body contains exactly `role` and
993	  `timestamp`: `{"role": "guest", "timestamp": "2026-01-01T00:00:00Z"}`; the
994	  service selects the latest snapshot whose `created_at` is not later than
995	  `timestamp` (the same selection as the bare-row lookup). On success it
996	  returns `{"dataset", "version", "snapshot_id", "created_at", "rows"}`; the
997	  `rows` are an order-preserving copy of the snapshot's rows masked exactly
998	  as the row-submission privacy view masks them, applying only the version's
999	  currently enabled policies (`redact`/`partial` semantics, `allowed_roles`,
1000	  nulls and uncovered fields behave identically). Every successful read
1001	  appends one masking-hit record per value actually masked, structurally
1002	  identical to the regular view's hit records and continuing the same
1003	  per-version sequence run, plus exactly one access record whose
1004	  `row_count` is the snapshot's row count and whose `masked_count` equals
1005	  the number of hit records written by the read. An empty snapshot, an
1006	  allowed role, all-null values and a version without policies all succeed
1007	  and leave only the access record. The records enter all existing
1008	  masking-hit/access reads, filters, summaries, diffs, reconciliation,
1009	  trends and cleanup previews; records of one read share a write timestamp,
1010	  sequences stay continuous across processes, and a write obstruction never
1011	  fails the read. The read never modifies or deletes the snapshot or its
1012	  rows and never changes policies or identification records. Unknown
1013	  dataset/version → `404`, and no snapshot existing at or before the
1014	  timestamp is likewise `404`, both checked before every shape check (the
1015	  latter whenever the body carries a usable timestamp); a missing or
1016	  wrong-typed `role`/`timestamp`, a role blank after trimming, an
1017	  unparseable or timezone-less timestamp, an extra body field, an empty,
1018	  whitespace-only or non-JSON body, a non-object body and any query
1019	  parameter are `422` and write nothing.
1020	- `GET /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/snapshots/{snapshot_id}/diff/{other_snapshot_id}` —
1021	  compare two snapshots as JSON-object multisets. Object key order does not
1022	  affect equality, while array order and JSON value types do (e.g. `1`, `1.0`,
1023	  `"1"` and `true` are all distinct), and duplicate rows are counted. Both
1024	  snapshots must belong to the dataset and version named in the path, otherwise
1025	  `422`; unknown dataset/version/snapshot → `404`. The response is
1026	  `{"from_snapshot_id", "to_snapshot_id", "added", "removed"}`; `added` lists
1027	  rows present more often (or only) in the `to` snapshot and `removed` the
1028	  converse, each entry being `{"row": {...}, "count": <int>}` sorted by the
1029	  canonical (key-sorted) JSON text of `row`.
1030	- `GET /datasets/{dataset}/snapshots/{base_snapshot_id}/diff/{target_snapshot_id}` —
1031	  read-only comparison of two snapshots belonging to two **different** schema
1032	  versions of the path dataset; the baseline snapshot is named first and the
1033	  target second, and either version order is allowed. It takes no request
1034	  body and no query parameters (`422`). Unknown dataset or snapshot → `404`,
1035	  checked ahead of every request-shape check; a snapshot owned by another
1036	  dataset, or two snapshots of the same schema version (same-version
1037	  comparisons still go through the snapshot-id diff endpoint) → `422`. The
1038	  JSON document is deterministic (fixed key order, compact whitespace,
1039	  exactly one trailing newline) with top-level keys `base_snapshot_id`,
1040	  `base_version`, `target_snapshot_id`, `target_version`, `field_changes`,
1041	  `added` and `removed` in that order. `field_changes` lists only additions,
1042	  removals, type changes and nullability changes of the two versions' field
1043	  definitions, reusing the compatibility/trajectory literals (`added`,
1044	  `removed`, `type_changed`, `nullable_tightened`, `nullable_loosened`);
1045	  several changes of one field collapse into a single entry (a type change
1046	  wins over a nullability change), entries sort by field name and each entry
1047	  has `field`, `kind`, `before` and `after`, with the missing side `null`
1048	  (never omitted). Rows are projected onto exactly the field names defined
1049	  in both versions — other stored keys and fields absent from a row do not
1050	  participate — and the projections are compared with the same-version
1051	  snapshot diff's multiset semantics (object key order irrelevant, array
1052	  order and value types significant, duplicates counted). `added` lists
1053	  rows present more often or only on the target side, `removed` the
1054	  converse, each entry `{"row", "count"}` sorted by the canonical
1055	  (key-sorted) JSON text of the projected row. The comparison is fully
1056	  read-only: snapshots, rows, field definitions, the lineage impact cache
1057	  and every privacy trail are never touched, and the result is identical
1058	  across process restarts.
1059	- `POST /datasets/{dataset}/versions/{version}/snapshots/{snapshot_id}/quality-rules/evaluate`
1060	  — evaluate the version's enabled quality rules over the snapshot's persisted
1061	  rows. The endpoint takes no request body and no query parameters (`422`);
